title: Are Facial Expressions Universal?
objective: After this level you can explain Paul Ekman's evidence for universal expressions and the current debate over it.
summary: Ekman's 1971 study with the Fore suggested some facial expressions are universal. Lisa Feldman Barrett argues they vary far more than that, and the debate continues.

cards.headline: A photo of a face, shown to people with little outside contact.
cards.body: In 1971, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen took photographs of faces to the Fore people of Papua New Guinea and asked a simple question: which face goes with this story? If people everywhere pick the same face, are expressions built in?

cards.headline: Ekman's case for universals
cards.body: Ekman and Friesen told short emotional stories and asked the Fore to choose the matching photographed face. Tasks like this, in small societies with little outside contact, gave strong evidence that people everywhere recognize the same expressions. Ekman's side adds that congenitally blind people, who never saw a face, move their faces much as sighted people do. Ekman's side lists seven: happiness, surprise, sadness, fear, disgust, contempt and anger.

cards.headline: Barrett's challenge
cards.body: In 2019, Lisa Feldman Barrett led a review that pushed back. Yes, people smile when happy and scowl when angry more often than chance. But how people express emotions varies a lot across cultures, situations and people. Most studies had people pick from a short list, which makes contrary evidence hard to find. Asked to name faces freely, people in small societies rarely gave the expected words. Trobriand Islanders read the wide-eyed gasp that Western studies call fear as a threat.

cards.headline: A debate still open
cards.body: Barrett proposes that emotions are constructed from experience, so one bodily state can become different emotions in different situations. The other side keeps finding support too: in 2021, Jessica Tracy's team reported that the Mayangna of Nicaragua recognized bodily expressions of anger, sadness and fear above chance. Both sides agree faces carry a lot of information. The argument is over how fixed and universal it is.

title: Does Smiling Make You Happier?
objective: After this level you can explain the facial feedback idea and why its replication record is mixed.
summary: The facial feedback idea says your expression can shape your feelings. The 1988 pen study failed a 17-lab replication, but deliberately posed smiles show a small effect.

cards.headline: Hold a pen between your teeth. Are cartoons funnier now?
cards.body: That was the claim of one of psychology's best-loved experiments. It rests on the facial feedback idea: that your face can affect the emotion you feel, not just show it. The pen test went into textbooks. Then many labs tried it again.

cards.headline: The pen study
cards.body: The facial feedback hypothesis says your expression can shape your emotion. In 1988, Fritz Strack and colleagues found a clever test. People held a pen in their mouth in ways that either engaged the smiling muscles or blocked them, without ever being asked to smile. Those in the smile position rated cartoons as funnier. No acting required, apparently.

cards.headline: Seventeen labs, almost nothing
cards.body: In 2016, 17 labs led by Eric-Jan Wagenmakers repeated the pen study, all following one shared protocol. In the original, the smile position made cartoons about 0.82 points funnier on a 10-point scale. Across the replications, the difference was 0.03. For the pen version, the effect all but vanished.

mascot.line: Keep the nuance: the pen study failed, but posed smiles still nudged happiness a little. Mixed is not the same as dead.

cards.headline: Many Smiles: a small nudge
cards.body: That wasn't the end. A 2019 meta-analysis led by Nicholas Coles found facial feedback has a small but highly variable effect. In 2022, the Many Smiles Collaboration, including researchers who disagreed, tested 3,878 people in 19 countries. Copying smiling faces or deliberately posing a smile raised happiness. The pen method was less conclusive.

title: The Sleep-Deprived Mind
objective: After this level you can explain how losing sleep affects mood, attention and judgment.
summary: Losing sleep dulls attention and judgment, often without you noticing, and makes the emotional brain overreact.

cards.headline: After 17 hours awake, you may test like someone who has been drinking.
cards.body: A short night leaves you groggy; everyone knows that. Less obvious is how far the damage reaches: into attention, judgment and even mood. And the strangest part is how little you may notice it.

cards.headline: Attention and judgment slip
cards.body: Sleep loss makes it harder to keep your attention on a task, make decisions and recall what you know, and the harm grows as sleep loss mounts. In a 2000 study, after 17 to 19 hours without sleep, performance on some tests was as bad as, or worse than, at a blood alcohol level of 0.05 percent. That's roughly an early start and a late night.

cards.headline: You can't feel how tired you are
cards.body: In a 2003 lab study, Hans Van Dongen and colleagues let adults spend 6 hours or less in bed a night for 14 days. Their thinking deficits built up to match up to 2 nights of no sleep at all. Yet their ratings of their own sleepiness rose only a little after the first days. Their scores kept falling; their sense of being fine didn't.

cards.headline: A shorter fuse
cards.body: Mood takes a hit too. In a 2007 brain-imaging study, Matthew Walker's team kept people awake about 35 hours, then showed them disturbing images. Their emotional brain centers were over 60 percent more reactive than in rested people. Walker's team concluded that without sleep, the brain struggles to put emotional experiences into context and respond in a controlled way.

title: What Dreams Say About You
objective: After this level you can explain what research on dream content shows and how it compares with Freud's dream interpretation.
summary: Freud read dreams for hidden meanings. Counting what happens in many dreams shows most dreams are ordinary, often negative, and follow the dreamer's waking concerns.

cards.headline: Freud read dreams like coded letters. What if you just count what's in them?
cards.body: Freud thought dreams hid a deeper meaning that an expert could decode. Later researchers tried something far less mysterious: collect lots of dreams and tally what actually happens in them. The two approaches don't agree.

cards.headline: Freud's hidden meanings
cards.body: Freud believed dreams opened a door to the unconscious. He split each dream in two. The manifest content is the storyline you remember: a chase, a party, a missed train. The latent content is the hidden meaning he believed lay beneath it. Remember Level 4? His evidence for such meanings was mostly his own interpretation.

mascot.line: This is Level 4's lesson again: counting what's in many dreams can be checked; one expert's reading can't.

cards.headline: Counting dreams
cards.body: Calvin Hall and Robert Van de Castle took a different route. They built a system for counting what happens in dreams, and in 1966 set norms from five dreams each of 100 men and 100 women students in Cleveland, Ohio. A study of 635 dream reports from a sleep lab found the typical dream is a clear, coherent story of a realistic situation, with the dreamer and other people doing very ordinary things.

cards.headline: Dreams follow your concerns
cards.body: The counts show dreams lean negative: 80 percent of men's and 77 percent of women's dreams in the norms hold at least one bad element, like aggression or misfortune, while 53 percent hold a good one. Dreams also track your general waking concerns and main relationships, though not the day's specific events. In one study by Rosalind Cartwright, women going through divorce who thought more about their former spouse dreamed about that person more often.

title: Fast Thinking, Slow Thinking
objective: After this level you can explain the two-systems idea of fast intuition and slow deliberation, and when each takes over.
summary: Psychologists describe a fast, automatic System 1 and a slow, deliberate System 2. The bat-and-ball puzzle shows how often the quick answer goes out unchecked.

cards.headline: A bat and a ball cost $1.10. The bat costs $1 more. What's the ball?
cards.body: Most people have an answer before they finish reading the question. Hold on to yours. This level is about where it came from, and why it is so often wrong.

cards.headline: Two ways of thinking
cards.body: Psychologists describe two modes of thought, which Keith Stanovich and Richard West labeled System 1 and System 2 in 2000. System 1 is fast, automatic, effortless and hard to control; it works much like perception, handing you answers you never asked for. System 2 is slower, effortful and deliberate. Most everyday judgments come from System 1, but System 2 can modify or override them. Daniel Kahneman, who shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics, built his account of judgment on this split.

mascot.line: Keep this one: fast answers aren't the problem. Unchecked fast answers are.

cards.headline: The checker that barely checks
cards.body: The answer that pops up is 10 cents: $1.10 splits neatly into $1 and 10 cents, and 10 cents feels about right for a ball. Check it, though: the bat has to cost a whole dollar more than the ball. The ball costs 5 cents. Shane Frederick found that 50 percent of Princeton students and 56 percent at the University of Michigan gave the wrong answer. System 2 is supposed to monitor System 1, but its monitoring is normally quite lax.

cards.headline: A test for the checker
cards.body: In 2005 Frederick turned the puzzle into one item of a three-item Cognitive Reflection Test. It measures the ability or disposition to reflect on a question and resist the first response that comes to mind. Scores relate to real choices about time and risk: people who go with the quick answer on such puzzles tend to be less patient about waiting for delayed rewards.

title: If It Comes to Mind, It Seems Common
objective: After this level you can explain the availability heuristic and why dramatic risks feel more likely than they are.
summary: The availability heuristic judges how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. That is why dramatic, widely reported risks feel more likely than quiet ones.

cards.headline: Which kills more people: tornadoes or asthma?
cards.body: In a 1978 study, college students said tornadoes. In the figures the researchers used, asthma was about 20 times more likely to kill. Why would bright people guess so badly?

cards.headline: A mental shortcut
cards.body: A heuristic is a mental shortcut, a rule of thumb that saves time and energy but isn't always the best way to decide. In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described three of them, including availability: judging how frequent or likely something is by the ease with which examples come to mind. Kahneman later explained heuristics as a quiet swap made by System 1: faced with a hard question, it answers an easier one. Here, "how common is it?" becomes "how easily can I think of cases?"

cards.headline: Easy to recall is not the same as common
cards.body: Try this: are there more English words that start with r, or that have r as the third letter? Most people say first, because words are easier to search by their first letter. Yet consonants such as r and k are actually more frequent in third position. In another test, people heard a list of famous men and women, then judged that the sex with the more famous names had more names on the list. It didn't.

cards.headline: Why dramatic risks feel bigger
cards.body: Back to the tornadoes. The 1978 study found the most overestimated causes of death were dramatic ones, such as botulism, tornadoes, floods and homicide. The underestimated ones, such as asthma, diabetes and stroke, were undramatic "quiet killers". The researchers traced the errors to how often and how memorably people meet each cause, including in the news. And when warned about these biases, people still couldn't correct them.

title: The First Number Wins
objective: After this level you can explain anchoring, using the experiment with a rigged wheel of fortune.
summary: An arbitrary number, like one from a rigged wheel of fortune, pulls later estimates toward it because people adjust too little. Anchoring has survived large replication tests.

cards.headline: A spinning wheel shouldn't change what you know about the world.
cards.body: In an experiment by Tversky and Kahneman, a wheel of fortune gave students a number before a question about African countries in the United Nations. The number was meaningless. It still moved their answers.

cards.headline: The rigged wheel
cards.body: The wheel was marked from 0 to 100 but rigged to stop only at 10 or 65. Students first said whether the percentage of African countries in the UN was higher or lower than their number, then gave their best guess. Those who saw 10 gave a median estimate of 25 percent; those who saw 65 gave 45. Paying people for accurate answers didn't shrink the effect.

cards.headline: Why the first number sticks
cards.body: Tversky and Kahneman called this anchoring: people start from a value and adjust, but the adjustment is typically too small. The anchor can even come from your own half-finished work. High school students given 5 seconds to estimate 8×7×6×5×4×3×2×1 gave a median of 2,250. Students shown 1×2×3×4×5×6×7×8 gave 512, because the first steps of that multiplication point lower. Both anchors dragged far below the true answer: 40,320.

cards.headline: A shortcut that passed the test
cards.body: Many famous findings have wobbled when retested. Anchoring hasn't. The Many Labs project, published in 2014, retested 13 classic and newer effects in 36 samples with 6,344 participants. Ten replicated consistently, and anchoring, tested with questions such as the height of Mount Everest, was among them.

title: The Linda Problem
objective: After this level you can explain the representativeness heuristic and how a good story can beat the odds in our judgment.
summary: Most people rate "bank teller and feminist" as likelier than "bank teller" for Linda, because she resembles the type. A later collaboration between rivals tested when the effect appears.

cards.headline: Meet Linda. She's 31, single, outspoken and very bright.
cards.body: She majored in philosophy. As a student she cared deeply about discrimination and social justice and joined antinuclear demonstrations. Which is more probable: Linda is a bank teller, or Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement?

cards.headline: The answer that feels right
cards.body: In Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 study, 85 percent of 142 students at the University of British Columbia picked "bank teller and feminist". But every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller, so the longer option can't be the more probable one. Probability & Statistics covers that rule. The psychology question is why the wrong answer feels so right.

cards.headline: Resemblance, not probability
cards.body: The representativeness heuristic judges something by how similar it seems to a stereotype or typical case. Linda resembles a feminist bank teller far more than a stereotypical bank teller. When one group ranked Linda's possible jobs by resemblance and another ranked them by probability, the two rankings matched almost perfectly. Asked "how likely?", people answered "how similar?"

mascot.line: Keep this: when rivals agree on the test before seeing the data, the data gets the last word.

cards.headline: Rivals who agreed on the test
cards.body: Not everyone accepted this. Ralph Hertwig argued that asking in frequencies removes the effect, and that people read "and" differently than intended. In 2001 he and Kahneman ran an adversarial collaboration: they agreed on the tests in advance, with Barbara Mellers as arbiter. Frequency formats alone did not remove the effect. With Hertwig's wording and no filler items, it disappeared. They still read the result differently.

title: The Halo Effect
objective: After this level you can explain the halo effect: how one good trait colors our judgment of everything else about a person.
summary: One overall impression colors how we rate everything else about a person. Thorndike named the halo effect in 1920, and Nisbett and Wilson showed people don't notice it.

cards.headline: Can a teacher's warmth change how you hear his accent?
cards.body: In a 1977 experiment, it did, and the students involved didn't notice. But the idea is older. It starts with army officers filling in rating forms.

cards.headline: A halo of general merit
cards.body: In 1920 Edward Thorndike examined army ratings. The plan asked officers to rate physique, intelligence, leadership and character, each judged independently. Yet one flight commander's ratings of 137 aviation cadets were far too closely linked: a man who seemed good overall looked good on everything. Thorndike called this constant error a "halo".

cards.headline: Same man, two moods
cards.body: Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson filmed two interviews with the same instructor, a French-speaking Belgian with a strong accent. In one he was warm and friendly; in the other, cold and distant. Students who saw the warm version rated his appearance, mannerisms and accent as appealing. Students who saw the cold version rated the very same features as irritating.

cards.headline: Blind to our own halo
cards.body: The students didn't realize their liking had changed their ratings. Those who saw the cold instructor even got the direction backward: they said disliking his traits had lowered their overall opinion of him. In fact, the overall impression came first and spread to the traits. A halo is hard to see from the inside.

title: Testing Only What You Believe
objective: After this level you can explain confirmation bias using Peter Wason's 2-4-6 number puzzle.
summary: In Peter Wason's 2-4-6 puzzle, most people test only number sets that fit their own guess, so they never learn it is too narrow. Klayman and Ha showed when that habit works and when it fails.

cards.headline: The numbers 2, 4, 6 follow a secret rule. Can you find it?
cards.body: You may try other sets of three numbers and hear whether each one fits. When you're sure, name the rule. In 1960 Peter Wason gave students exactly this puzzle.

cards.headline: Testing the guess you already have
cards.body: Most people guess something like "increasing by 2" and test sets such as 6, 8, 10. Each one fits, so confidence climbs. But the rule was simply increasing numbers. In Wason's study, only 6 of 29 students named the right rule without first announcing a wrong one.

cards.headline: Why "yes" never helped
cards.body: Joshua Klayman and Young-won Ha spelled out the trap in 1987. If your guess is "increasing by 2", every set that fits it also fits "increasing", so testing only fitting sets can never show your guess is wrong. Only a set you expect to fail, like 2, 4, 7, can surprise you. Wason read his results as a preference for confirming evidence over evidence that could eliminate an idea.

cards.headline: A good shortcut in the wrong place
cards.body: Klayman and Ha called this habit a positive test strategy, and argued it isn't simply a flaw. Under realistic conditions it can be a very good heuristic for checking a hypothesis. It leads to systematic errors when the true rule is broader than your guess, which is exactly how Wason built his puzzle.

title: I Knew It All Along
objective: After this level you can explain hindsight bias and how researchers caught people rewriting their own predictions.
summary: After an outcome is known, people feel it was predictable and even misremember their own forecasts. Fischhoff and Beyth caught it with predictions about Nixon's trips.

cards.headline: Did you know it all along? Your memory may be editing the answer.
cards.body: Before President Richard Nixon's trips to Beijing and Moscow, psychologists asked people to predict what would happen. Then they waited for history, and asked again.

cards.headline: Rewriting your own forecast
cards.body: Baruch Fischhoff and Ruth Beyth had people judge the probability of various outcomes of Nixon's trips. Afterward, the same people tried to recall the probabilities they had given. Their memories slanted toward what happened: they remembered giving higher odds to events that occurred and lower odds to events that didn't. The title of their 1975 paper says it all: "I knew it would happen."

cards.headline: Why hindsight feels so convincing
cards.body: Hindsight bias is believing an event was more predictable after it happened than it was before. Neal Roese and Kathleen Vohs trace it to three sources. We recall the facts that fit the outcome and build a story around them. The ease of understanding what happened gets mistaken for how likely it was. And we like a world that seems orderly and predictable. Telling people to ignore what they know doesn't remove it.

cards.headline: Everywhere, with a cost
cards.body: Hindsight bias has been featured in more than 800 scholarly papers. It shows up in people around the world, young and old, in areas from medical diagnoses to terrorist attacks. It has a cost: it feeds overconfidence in how certain our judgments are. One remedy helps, though: deliberately considering other explanations for how things turned out.

title: Overconfidence and Dunning-Kruger
objective: After this level you can explain overconfidence research and why the Dunning-Kruger effect is debated.
summary: Most people rate their own skills above the median. Kruger and Dunning reported that the least skilled overrate themselves most, but critics argue much of that pattern is a statistical artifact.

cards.headline: Are you a better driver than the median driver? Most drivers think so.
cards.body: At most half of any group can be above its median. So what is going on when far more than half of a group rate themselves better than that?

cards.headline: Nearly everyone is above average
cards.body: In a study published in 1981, Ola Svenson asked students in the United States and Sweden to compare their driving skill with others in their group. In the US sample, 93 percent believed they were more skillful than the median driver; in the Swedish sample, 69 percent did. It fits a wider pattern: people tend to hold overly favorable views of their abilities in many areas.

cards.headline: Unskilled and unaware?
cards.body: In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning tested people on humor, grammar and logic. Those in the bottom quarter scored around the 12th percentile but estimated themselves at the 62nd. The authors argued that the skills you need to do well are the same ones you need to notice you're doing badly. The finding became famous as the Dunning-Kruger effect.

cards.headline: A trick of the chart?
cards.body: Critics argue much of the effect comes from the usual way of showing it: averaging self-ratings for four ability groups. That chart is muddied by the better-than-average tendency and a statistical quirk called regression toward the mean. In 2020 Gilles Gignac and Marcin Zajenkowski tested 929 people on intelligence with other methods, found no support for the pattern, and concluded the effect may be much smaller than reported.

title: Priming: A Famous Finding Falls
objective: After this level you can explain which priming effects hold up and why the "slow walking" priming study failed to replicate.
summary: The famous finding that old-age words make people walk slowly failed a careful replication that pointed to experimenters' expectations. Word priming, by contrast, holds up well.

cards.headline: Can reading words about old age make you walk more slowly?
cards.body: A famous 1996 study said yes, and it became a textbook classic. Then a team checked it with better equipment.

cards.headline: The slow-walking study
cards.body: John Bargh and colleagues had students unscramble sentences. For some, the words were linked to old age. Afterward, those students walked more slowly down the hallway when leaving, the researchers reported, without noticing the link. The study helped spread a big idea in social psychology: that much of our behavior is steered by influences we aren't aware of.

cards.headline: Checked with infrared
cards.body: In 2012 Stéphane Doyen and colleagues in Brussels repeated the study with a larger sample. Instead of a hand-held stopwatch, a method prone to error and bias, hidden infrared sensors timed the walkers. They found no priming effect. In a second experiment, walkers slowed only when the experimenters had been led to expect it. The experimenters' expectations, it seems, helped make the effect.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: word priming holds up well. It's the dramatic claims about steering behavior that fell.

cards.headline: What priming does hold up
cards.body: Priming itself isn't a myth. In word priming, a word such as cat automatically activates related ideas such as dog, so a related word is recognized faster when it follows. The Semantic Priming Project built the largest database of these effects. What fell were bigger claims about behavior: in Level 53's Many Labs project, flag priming and currency priming also failed to replicate.

title: Checkpoint: Mental Shortcuts
objective: After this level you can explain why the mind uses shortcuts and how the research showed where they go wrong.
summary: Heuristics save time and effort and usually work, but their errors are systematic. That is how researchers caught them, and why some findings held up while others fell.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: why would a smart mind cut corners?
cards.body: You've watched shortcuts misfire, from a rigged wheel to a slow walk down a hallway. Now the bigger picture: why the mind uses them at all, and how researchers caught them in the act.

cards.headline: Useful, but predictably wrong
cards.body: Tversky and Kahneman put it plainly in 1974: in general, heuristics are quite useful, but sometimes they lead to severe and systematic errors. A rule of thumb saves time and energy, even though it isn't always the best method. Klayman and Ha said the same about testing ideas: the positive test strategy is often a very good heuristic under realistic conditions.

cards.headline: Caught by their mistakes
cards.body: How do you study a shortcut you can't see? By its errors. Kahneman explained that heuristics were identified by the characteristic errors they cause, and because those errors are systematic, they are predictable. Set up a question where the shortcut and the right answer part ways, then watch which one people give. The wheel, Linda and the 2-4-6 puzzle all work that way.

title: Comfort Over Food
objective: After this level you can explain what Harry Harlow's monkey studies showed about attachment and why they are ethically criticized.
summary: Harlow's infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother that gave no milk, showing comfort, not food, anchors attachment. The studies are now widely judged unethical and even cruel.

cards.headline: A baby monkey could choose: the mother with milk, or the soft one.
cards.body: Scientists generally used to think babies bond with whoever feeds them. Food first, love as a side effect. In the 1950s, Harry Harlow put that idea to a blunt test with infant monkeys. What they chose changed how psychologists think about attachment, and it came at a cost.

cards.headline: Wire with milk, or cloth with nothing
cards.body: Harlow separated newborn monkeys from their mothers and gave each two stand-in mothers. One was bare wire mesh and could give milk. The other was covered in soft cloth and gave none. If food builds the bond, the wire mother should win. She didn't. The infants spent their time clinging to the cloth mother and went to the wire one only when they needed to feed. The wire mother was a snack bar; the cloth one was home.

mascot.line: Keep this one: in these studies, attachment rested on comfort and security, not just on who brought the food.

cards.headline: Comfort is the point
cards.body: The pattern held when the monkeys were scared. Faced with frightening objects such as a moving toy bear, the infants sought out the soft mother, whichever one fed them. Harlow presented these findings in 1958 in "The Nature of Love", his address as president of the American Psychological Association. His conclusion: comfort and security, not nourishment alone, are critical to the bond between infant and mother.

cards.headline: The price the monkeys paid
cards.body: The same studies raise hard questions. Harlow ran them before modern ethics guidelines existed, and today they are widely considered unethical and even cruel. Taking newborns from their mothers was the method itself. In a 1997 article, John Gluck called Harlow an ethical paradox: his work showed that monkeys have rich inner lives full of emotion, yet he was criticized for ignoring what his own findings implied.

title: Secure and Insecure Attachment

summary: Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation watches how toddlers react when a caregiver leaves and returns. It sorts attachment into secure, avoidant and resistant types, with disorganized added later.

cards.headline: A stranger walks in. The parent walks out. Watch the baby.
cards.body: Harlow showed that comfort builds a bond. But do all children bond the same way? In 1970, Mary Ainsworth published a short, carefully staged scene designed to find out. The telling moments are the goodbye, and the hello that follows.

cards.headline: The Strange Situation
cards.body: Ainsworth built on John Bowlby's idea of a secure base: a caregiver whose presence lets a child feel safe enough to explore. In her Strange Situation, a caregiver and a young child spend time in a room with toys. A stranger comes in, the caregiver leaves the child with the stranger, then returns a few minutes later. Ainsworth sorted children by how they responded to the separation and to the reunion.

title: Piaget's Stages
objective: After this level you can explain Jean Piaget's stages of thinking and where later research found children more capable.
summary: Piaget described four stages of thinking, from the sensorimotor stage to formal operations. Looking-time studies later showed babies understand hidden objects months earlier than he thought.

cards.headline: Pour juice into a taller glass, and a young child may say there is more.
cards.body: Nothing was added; only the shape changed. Jean Piaget built a famous theory on mistakes like this one, arguing that children don't think like small adults. Later research kept his big idea, but found that babies know more than he gave them credit for.

events.label: Sensorimotor: learning through senses and movement
Preoperational: pretend play and symbols, no conservation yet
Concrete operational: logic about real things; conservation
Formal operational: abstract and hypothetical thinking

cards.headline: The toy under the blanket
cards.body: Piaget's tests were simple. To check object permanence, the sense that things still exist out of sight, he hid a toy under a blanket. Infants who had it reached for the toy; in his view, younger ones didn't remember it once it was hidden. Conservation came later: in the concrete operational stage, children know water poured from a tall, thin glass into a short, fat one is the same amount. Each stage, for Piaget, was a new way of reasoning, not just more facts.

cards.headline: Babies who knew more than they showed
cards.body: Reaching, it turns out, lags behind knowing. Infants as young as 3.5 months seem to understand that hidden objects still exist, yet they don't search for them until 7 to 8 months. Renée Baillargeon measured looking instead. In a 1991 study with Julie DeVos, 3.5-month-olds watched a tall carrot slide behind a screen with a window. It should have shown in the window but didn't, and the babies looked reliably longer. Many studies now suggest children reach milestones earlier, and change more gradually, than Piaget described.

title: Knowing Others Have Minds
objective: After this level you can explain theory of mind and the false-belief test used to show when children develop it.
summary: Theory of mind is understanding that others can think and believe differently from you. False-belief tests like the Sally-Anne task show it arrives around age 4 to 5, at a similar age across cultures.

cards.headline: Anne moves Sally's marble while Sally is away. Where will Sally look?
cards.body: You know the marble moved. Sally doesn't. Getting the answer right means holding two versions of the world in mind: what is true, and what Sally believes. Young children often get it wrong, and the age when they start getting it right tells psychologists something big.

cards.headline: Minds that differ from yours
cards.body: Theory of mind is understanding that other people have thoughts, feelings and beliefs different from your own. Children develop it between about 3 and 5 years old. Psychologists usually spot it with false-belief tasks, which test whether a child understands that someone else can believe something that isn't true. You can't see a belief, so the test has to make one visible.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: passing isn't about knowing where the marble is. It's knowing that Sally doesn't.

cards.headline: The Sally-Anne task
cards.body: In one classic false-belief test, a child watches a short scene. Sally puts her marble away and leaves. While she's gone, Anne moves the marble into her own box. Then comes the key question: where will Sally look for her marble? Past the age of 4 to 5, most children say Sally will look where she left it. In early studies, younger children systematically got it wrong, as if Sally must know what they know.

cards.headline: Same milestone, many cultures
cards.body: Is this a quirk of Western children? In 2005, Tara Callaghan and colleagues gave one standard false-belief test to children in Canada, India, Peru, Samoa and Thailand. In every culture, children passed at about age 5. A 2001 review of 178 studies, led by Henry Wellman, found the same shift across countries: preschoolers go from below-chance to above-chance on false-belief tasks.

title: How Babies Crack Language
objective: After this level you can explain how infants pick out words and why language is easiest to learn early.
summary: Babies find words by tracking which sounds follow which, and start out hearing many languages' sounds. An early start gives a lasting edge in grammar.

cards.headline: Nobody hands a baby a dictionary. So how do babies find the words?
cards.body: Adults hear speech as separate words, but to a baby it arrives as fluent, running sound. Finding where one word ends and the next begins is a basic task of learning a language. Babies manage it anyway, and research shows both how they do it and why starting early helps.

cards.headline: Babies who keep score
cards.body: In 1996, Jenny Saffran, Richard Aslin and Elissa Newport tested whether 8-month-old infants could pull words out of fluent speech. The only clue was statistical: which sounds tended to follow which. After just 2 minutes of listening, the babies could pick out the words. Nobody explained anything to them. Infants, it seems, keep track of patterns in what they hear.

cards.headline: Tuned to home
cards.body: Young infants can tell apart many speech sounds, whatever language they hear at home. In a 1981 study led by Janet Werker, 7-month-olds told apart two pairs of Hindi speech sounds, while English-speaking adults had trouble with the rarer pair. Patricia Kuhl has proposed a reason: the brain commits early to the sound patterns it experiences, which might explain why infants learn language better than adults.

cards.headline: Earlier is easier
cards.body: Age keeps mattering after infancy. In 1989, Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport tested the English grammar of 46 Korean and Chinese speakers who had moved to the United States between ages 3 and 39. The earlier people arrived, the better they scored, right up to puberty. After that, scores were low, varied widely and no longer tracked arrival age. When it comes to grammar, earlier really was easier.

title: The Marshmallow Test
objective: After this level you can explain the delay-of-gratification studies and what a 2018 replication changed about their meaning.
summary: Preschoolers who waited longer for a treat grew into more competent teens in Mischel's studies. A 2018 replication found the link far weaker once family background was counted.

cards.headline: One marshmallow now, or more if you can wait?
cards.body: It's one of psychology's most famous tests. Early studies suggested that 4-year-olds who waited longer grew into more successful teenagers. Then, in 2018, researchers tried it again with 918 children. The treat stayed the same; the story changed.

cards.headline: The waiting game
cards.body: In Walter Mischel's studies, a preschooler sat alone with a treat such as a marshmallow. Eat it now, or wait for the adult to come back and get more. The children attended a preschool on the Stanford University campus. Mischel's team followed them up, and 4-year-olds who waited longer grew into more competent adolescents who did better at school. Self-control, it seemed, could be measured with a sweet.

cards.fact: In a 2018 replication, waiting at age 4 predicted teen achievement only half as strongly as before.
cards.context: The original long-term links rested on small, highly selective samples of 35 to 89 children from the Stanford community. Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan retested the idea with 918 children from a larger, more diverse sample. Focusing on children whose mothers hadn't finished college, the link to achievement at 15 was half the original size.

cards.headline: What the waiting was standing in for
cards.body: Then the researchers accounted for family background, early cognitive ability and the home environment. The link shrank by about two thirds. Much of what looked like the power of waiting traveled with a child's circumstances and early skills. The famous finding didn't vanish, but it shrank sharply: one test at age 4 is a weak crystal ball.

title: Why Teens Take More Risks
objective: After this level you can explain how the presence of peers raises teenagers' risk taking in experiments.
summary: Teens take more risks when peers are present or watching, far more than adults do, and being watched boosts reward-related brain activity in teens.

cards.headline: Teens don't take most of their risks alone.
cards.body: Most risk taking by adolescents happens with other teens around. Is that just because teens spend time with friends, or does an audience change the decision itself? Psychologists brought the question into the lab, with a driving game.

cards.headline: Alone, or with two friends
cards.body: In 2005, Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg tested 306 people in three age groups: 13 to 16, 18 to 22, and 24 and over. Each was randomly assigned to do risk tasks alone or with two peers of the same age. One task was "Chicken", a video driving game: stop the car when the light turns yellow, or push on. Everyone took more risks in a group, but the peer effect was stronger for teens and young adults than for adults.

cards.headline: Watched from the next room
cards.body: Peers don't even need to be in the room. In a 2011 study led by Jason Chein, people played a simulated driving game during brain scans, once alone and once while peers watched from an adjacent room. Watched teens took more risks; adults didn't. Only the teens showed extra activity in reward-related brain areas, and it predicted their risky choices. An audience seems to make the payoff of a risky move look bigger.

cards.headline: Risky with friends is not the same as troubled
cards.body: None of this paints teenagers as broken. Most teens don't go through the extreme "storm and stress" that the pioneer G. Stanley Hall once suggested. Only small numbers have major conflicts with their parents, and most arguments are about everyday things like homework and chores.

title: Erikson's Life Stages
objective: After this level you can explain Erik Erikson's stages of development from infancy to old age.
summary: Erik Erikson turned Freud's childhood theory into eight psychosocial stages across the whole lifespan, each with its own task, from trust in infancy to integrity in old age.

cards.headline: Freud thought personality was shaped in childhood. Erikson kept going.
cards.body: Erik Erikson took Freud's theory and stretched it across the whole of life. In his view, every age brings its own big task, from a baby learning to trust to an older adult looking back. Which one are you working on now?

cards.headline: Social, and lifelong
cards.body: Erikson turned Freud's ideas into a psychosocial theory: how we interact with other people shapes our sense of self. And where Freud believed personality is shaped only in childhood, Erikson said it keeps developing across the lifespan. He described eight stages from infancy to late adulthood. Each has a conflict or task to work through, and resolving it brings a sense of competence.

Intimacy vs. isolation: building close relationships

Integrity vs. despair: looking back on a life

mascot.line: You don't need every age range. Remember the arc: trust in infancy, identity in adolescence, integrity in late life.

cards.headline: The tasks of adulthood
cards.body: Three of the eight stages belong to adults. Intimacy comes first, and Erikson said it needs a strong sense of self. Generativity means finding your life's work and contributing to others, through volunteering, mentoring or raising children. Integrity versus despair closes the list: looking back on life with a sense of satisfaction, or of failure. Growing up, for Erikson, never quite finishes.

title: Older and Happier?
objective: After this level you can explain which mental abilities fade with age, which grow, and why older adults often report more contentment.
summary: Crystallized knowledge holds steady with age while fluid reasoning slows. Emotional life often grows more positive and stable, as socioemotional selectivity theory explains.

cards.headline: Growing old sounds like losing things. The research tells a more mixed story.
cards.body: Some mental abilities do slow with age. Others hold steady or even improve. And when researchers checked people's feelings throughout ordinary days, getting older came out ahead in an unexpected way.

mascot.line: People often assume every ability fades with age. Knowledge and skills built over a lifetime tend to hold steady.

cards.headline: What slows, what stays
cards.body: Psychologists split intelligence into two kinds. Crystallized intelligence is what you've gathered through experience: information, skills and strategies. It tends to hold steady with age and may even improve. Fluid intelligence covers processing, reasoning and memory, and in late adulthood it begins to decline as these processes slow. Research has also found that adults who stay mentally active show less cognitive decline. Knowing tends to stay; speed tends to fade.

cards.headline: Feelings, caught in the moment
cards.body: Laura Carstensen's team took an unusual approach. Adults of all ages reported how they felt at five random moments a day, for a week. The team repeated the week 5 and 10 years later. Growing older went with more positive emotional well-being and steadier emotions, even after accounting for personality, health and demographics.

cards.headline: When time feels shorter
cards.body: Carstensen's explanation is socioemotional selectivity theory. When time ahead feels shorter, emotional goals become more important than other goals. That shift comes with age, but also with moving away, illness or war. It shows up in friendships: with age, social circles tend to shrink in number, while the friends who remain stay as close, or closer.

title: Asch's Lines
objective: After this level you can explain Solomon Asch's conformity experiments and what made people more or less likely to go along.
summary: In Asch's 1950s line studies, about three in four people went along with an obviously wrong group answer at least once. One ally or a private answer weakened the pull.

cards.headline: Which line matches? Easy, until everyone else answers first.
cards.body: In the 1950s, Solomon Asch gave groups a vision test a child could pass. The catch was the other people at the table. What made careful adults say something they could see was false, and what set them free?

cards.headline: The rigged vision test
cards.body: Asch showed a target line and three others, and each person said aloud which one matched. Only one person at the table was a real participant. The rest were confederates, people working for the researcher, and on some trials they all named an obviously wrong line. Then the real participant had to answer. In Asch's 1955 report, 76 percent went along with the wrong answer at least once. Three in four, on a test a child could pass.

mascot.line: People mix up agreeing and going along. Asch's participants mostly went along: the words changed, the belief didn't.

cards.headline: Saying it without believing it
cards.body: Conformity means changing your behavior to go along with a group, even when you disagree. Asch's participants weren't confused. The task was easy, so they didn't need the group for information. They said the wrong answer out loud while privately not accepting it, to fit in and avoid ridicule. Psychologists call that normative social influence: going along to get along.

title: Milgram's Shock Machine
objective: After this level you can explain Stanley Milgram's obedience studies, their main criticisms and later partial replications.
summary: In Milgram's best-known version, 65 percent obeyed to the top shock. Archives show lower obedience across versions and doubting participants; a 2009 replication still found similar obedience.

cards.headline: Would you shock a stranger because a man in a lab coat said so?
cards.body: Stanley Milgram, a professor at Yale, wanted to test the defense of Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann: he was just following orders. The experiment he built became one of psychology's most famous, and one of its most argued over.

cards.headline: The shock machine
cards.body: In Milgram's 1963 study, 40 men were told they were helping with research on learning. Each was to shock a learner for wrong answers, stepping up 15 volts at a time to 450 volts. The learner was a confederate and felt nothing, but the men didn't know that. When the experimenter told them to continue, 65 percent kept going to the very last switch.

cards.headline: Change the room, change the obedience
cards.body: Milgram kept changing the setup. With the learner in the same room as the teacher, obedience fell to 40 percent. When the experimenter gave orders by phone, it fell further. The pattern: the more human the victim felt, and the weaker the authority seemed, the more people refused.

cards.headline: What the archives show
cards.body: The famous 65 percent was one version, not the rule. A 2014 synthesis led by Nick Haslam counted 23 versions; across 21 of them, 43.6 percent went to the maximum. And an unpublished analysis by Milgram's assistant Taketo Murata, reported by Gina Perry's team in 2020, found that in 18 of 23 versions, people who fully believed the shocks were real gave lower shocks than doubters.

cards.headline: Still obeying in 2009
cards.body: In 2009 Jerry Burger published a partial replication. To protect participants, his 70 adults went only as far as 150 volts, the learner's first spoken protest. Obedience was only slightly lower than in Milgram's day. The criticisms are real, and so is the core finding: many people still obey.

title: The Stanford Prison Experiment
objective: After this level you can explain what the 1971 study claimed and why critics say it does not show what it claimed.
summary: The 1971 Stanford study was taught as proof that roles make people cruel. Archives show the guards were coached, and a 2006 study without guard guidelines turned out differently.

cards.headline: A mock prison, 24 students, six days. The lesson may be wrong.
cards.body: In 1971, a study at Stanford seemed to show that ordinary students turn cruel once they put on a guard's uniform. It became a textbook classic. Then researchers went through the archives.

cards.headline: The story as told
cards.body: In August 1971, Philip Zimbardo's team picked 24 healthy male college students from more than 70 volunteers and randomly assigned them to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison. The study was meant to run for weeks but ended after six days, with guards turning abusive and prisoners in severe distress. It became a famous demonstration that roles and situations can make ordinary people cruel.

cards.headline: The guards were coached
cards.body: At the guards' orientation, Zimbardo told them they could create fear and a sense of powerlessness in the prisoners. That's a job description, not a blank slate. Recordings in the archives go further: the warden, an undergraduate named David Jaffe, pressed a gentle guard to act as a "tough guard".

cards.headline: Opening the archives
cards.body: In 2018 the French researcher Thibault Le Texier published a book built on the study's archives, then a 2019 article in American Psychologist. He reported that guards received precise instructions and that data collection was biased and incomplete. He argues Zimbardo designed the study from the start as a demonstration of the harm prisons do, not as a neutral test.

cards.headline: Run it again, without the script
cards.body: In the BBC Prison Study, published in 2006, Stephen Reicher and Alex Haslam randomly assigned men to be guards or prisoners too, but gave the guards no guidelines. The participants did not automatically slip into their roles. Take away the coaching, and the story that people naturally become cruel looks much weaker.

title: Why Bystanders Hesitate
objective: After this level you can explain the bystander effect and why the famous story of 38 silent witnesses was wrong.
summary: Each person is less likely to help when others are present, because responsibility feels shared. The famous story of 38 silent witnesses was wrong, and in real conflicts someone usually helps.

cards.headline: The famous story says 38 neighbors watched and did nothing.
cards.body: In 1964, Kitty Genovese was murdered in New York, and the story spread that none of her many neighbors helped. It launched a whole field of research. The research held up. The story didn't.

cards.headline: More listeners, fewer helpers
cards.body: In 1968, John Darley and Bibb Latane had students talk over an intercom. Then one voice seemed to have a seizure. Of those who thought they alone heard it, 85 percent reported it before the fit ended; of those who thought four others were listening, 31 percent did. That's the bystander effect, and diffusion of responsibility explains it: when many could help, the duty spreads thin.

cards.headline: What the archives say
cards.body: In 2007, Rachel Manning and colleagues went back to the records. They found no evidence that 38 witnesses were present, that witnesses saw the murder, or that they all stayed inactive. One man shouted at the attacker, and a woman said she called the police. The story psychology retold for decades was mostly wrong.

mascot.line: Keep both halves: each person holds back a bit in a crowd, yet someone in the crowd usually steps in.

cards.headline: Real emergencies, real help
cards.body: A 2011 meta-analysis led by Peter Fischer found the bystander effect is weaker when an emergency is clearly dangerous. Then Richard Philpot's team studied 219 real public conflicts caught on security cameras in the UK, the Netherlands and South Africa. In 9 of 10, at least one bystander did something to help, and more bystanders made help more likely.

title: Blaming the Person, Not the Situation
objective: After this level you can explain the fundamental attribution error and the experiment that first showed it.
summary: We tend to explain other people's behavior by their character and overlook the situation. Jones and Harris's 1967 essay study and the 1977 quizmaster study caught this in the lab.

cards.headline: When others snap, it's their personality. When you do, it was a bad day.
cards.body: We judge people constantly, and we tend to explain what they do by who they are, underestimating the situation they're in. Psychologists have a grand name for it and some clever experiments that caught it.

cards.headline: Person or situation?
cards.body: Behavior can be explained by the situation, your surroundings in the moment, or by disposition, inner traits like personality. Social psychologists have tended to stress the situation, and personality psychologists the person; modern approaches weigh both. The fundamental attribution error is our habit of blaming other people's traits while underestimating the power of their situation.

cards.headline: The Castro essays
cards.body: In 1967, Edward Jones and Victor Harris had Duke University students read an essay for or against Fidel Castro's Cuba. Some readers were told a course instructor had assigned the writer's side. Even so, readers tended to judge the writer's true opinion as matching the essay. They knew the writer had no choice, and they judged the person anyway.

cards.headline: The quizmaster's unfair edge
cards.body: In a 1977 study by Lee Ross and colleagues, students were randomly assigned to be questioners or contestants. Questioners wrote hard questions they knew the answers to. Afterward, contestants and observers rated the questioners as more knowledgeable, overlooking the obvious advantage of writing your own quiz.

cards.headline: Kinder to ourselves
cards.body: Turn the lens around, and the classic idea says the pattern flips: we explain our own behavior by the situation (I was tired, the exam was unfair) but other people's by their character. That's the actor-observer bias. But a 2006 review of 173 studies by Bertram Malle found little support for it overall; the pattern showed up mainly when explaining bad outcomes, like failures and mistakes.

learned: We overrate traits and underrate situations in others

Quizmasters seemed smarter despite writing the questions

title: Changing Your Mind to Fit Your Actions
objective: After this level you can explain cognitive dissonance using Leon Festinger's one-dollar experiment.
summary: Clashing beliefs and actions feel uncomfortable, so people often change the belief. Students paid 1 dollar to call a dull task fun came to like it more than those paid 20.

cards.headline: Pay people less, and they'll like the boring job more?
cards.body: In 1959, two psychologists paid students either 1 dollar or 20 dollars to tell a small lie about a dull task. Afterward, the students who got 1 dollar said they liked the task more. The reason is one of social psychology's big ideas.

cards.headline: The itch of inconsistency
cards.body: Leon Festinger called it cognitive dissonance: the discomfort of holding attitudes, beliefs or actions that clash. You believe smoking is harmful, yet you smoke. Something has to give. You can change the behavior, change the belief, or add a new justification that smooths things over. Often the belief is the easiest thing to move.

cards.headline: An hour of spools and pegs
cards.body: In Festinger and Carlsmith's 1959 experiment, students spent an hour on deliberately dull tasks: filling a tray with spools, emptying it, filling it again, then turning square pegs a quarter turn at a time. Then each was paid 1 dollar or 20 dollars to tell a waiting student that the tasks were enjoyable.

mascot.line: Keep this twist: a small reward left no excuse, so the belief had to change instead.

cards.headline: The one-dollar surprise
cards.body: Later, students paid 1 dollar rated the tasks as more enjoyable than students paid 20 dollars, whose ratings were close to a control group that told no one anything. Festinger and Carlsmith's explanation: 20 dollars was a good enough reason to tell the lie. One dollar wasn't. So the low-paid students eased their dissonance by deciding the tasks were fun after all.

cards.headline: Suffering for it makes it worth it
cards.body: Effort works the same way. In a 1959 experiment by Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills, students who went through a difficult initiation to join a deliberately dull discussion group rated it more favorably than those with an easy initiation or none. If it cost you that much, it must be good.

title: Two Roads to Persuasion
objective: After this level you can explain the central and peripheral routes to persuasion and when each one works.
summary: Messages persuade by their arguments (the central route) or by cues like who is speaking (the peripheral route). Students affected by a proposal weighed its arguments; others followed the source.

cards.headline: Same speech, same speaker. One date decided what mattered.
cards.body: In 1981, psychologists played students a speech proposing a tough new exam for seniors. Some heard strong arguments, some weak ones; some were told it came from experts, some from a high school class. What students cared about depended on when the exam would start.

cards.headline: Two roads
cards.body: Persuasion is changing an attitude through communication. Richard Petty and John Cacioppo's elaboration likelihood model says it travels two roads. The central route runs through thoughtful consideration of the arguments. The peripheral route runs through cues around the message, like an attractive speaker or a celebrity endorsement.

cards.headline: The exam experiment
cards.body: In the 1981 experiment by Petty, Cacioppo and Rachel Goldman, University of Missouri students heard a message proposing senior comprehensive exams. The arguments were strong or weak. The source was said to be a commission chaired by a Princeton professor, or a local high school class. Half were told the exams would start next year; half, in 10 years.

cards.headline: Care, and you check the arguments
cards.body: When the exams would start the following year, landing on the students themselves, their attitudes depended mainly on argument quality. When the exams were 10 years away, attitudes depended mainly on the source's expertise. The central route works when people are motivated and able to think, and it tends to produce lasting change; peripheral-route change is usually less permanent.

title: Us Versus Them
objective: After this level you can explain in-group favoritism and how the minimal group studies produced it from almost nothing.
summary: We prefer our in-groups. Tajfel's minimal group studies showed that boys sorted into groups on trivial, actually random grounds still favored their own group, even at a cost.

cards.headline: Pick a painting. Congratulations, you now have a team.
cards.body: Around 1970, Henri Tajfel told schoolboys in Bristol that they had been grouped by which of two painters they preferred. The groups meant nothing; he had actually assigned them at random. Would the boys still take sides?

cards.headline: Us and them
cards.body: An in-group is a group you identify with; an out-group is one you see as different from you. The groups we belong to are a powerful source of identity and self-esteem, so we tend to feel good about them. In-group bias is the result: a preference for our own group over other groups.

cards.headline: Klee or Kandinsky?
cards.body: In experiments at the University of Bristol reported in 1970, Tajfel divided boys aged 14 and 15 into groups on trivial grounds, such as preferring paintings by Paul Klee or Wassily Kandinsky. In fact, the boys were assigned at random. No history, no rivalry, nothing to fight over.

cards.headline: Winning by a wider margin
cards.body: Next, each boy shared out points worth real money between other boys, identified only by code number and group, and never to himself. Most boys gave more to their own group. Often they chose the biggest gap in their group's favor, even when that meant their own group got less overall. Beating them mattered more than having more.

cards.headline: Almost nothing is enough
cards.body: Tajfel concluded that the mere fact of being divided into groups can be enough to trigger discrimination, even without any conflict of interests or past hostility.

title: Culture and the WEIRD Problem
objective: After this level you can explain how culture shapes thinking and why findings from WEIRD samples may not apply everywhere.
summary: Much of psychology comes from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic samples, which are often outliers. Culture shapes what people notice and how they explain behavior.

cards.headline: Much of what psychology calls human nature came from a thin slice of humanity.
cards.body: In 2010, three researchers gave that slice a memorable name: WEIRD. Their question was simple and awkward. If most participants come from one kind of society, whose mind has psychology been describing?

cards.headline: Who counts as everyone?
cards.body: Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan argued that behavioral scientists often make broad claims about human nature from samples drawn entirely from WEIRD societies: Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic. Reviewing studies across many populations, they found results varied a lot, and WEIRD participants were often outliers, among the least representative people to generalize from.

cards.fact: Americans are less than 5 percent of the world's people, yet they were the main focus of top psychology journals.
cards.context: In 2008, Jeffrey Arnett showed that research in six leading journals of the American Psychological Association focused mostly on Americans.

cards.headline: Same fish tank, different view
cards.body: In a 2001 study, Takahiko Masuda and Richard Nisbett showed Japanese and American participants animated underwater scenes. Asked what they saw, the Japanese made more statements about the background and the relationships in the scene. Same fish, different focus.

mascot.line: This connects back: even a famous bias can change size when you cross a border. Always ask who was studied.

cards.headline: Blame travels differently
cards.body: Remember the fundamental attribution error from Level 75? It isn't equally strong everywhere. People from individualistic cultures, such as the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom, commit it more than people from collectivistic cultures, which focus more on relationships and the group.

cards.headline: Obeying a cause, not an order
cards.body: Alex Haslam and Stephen Reicher reanalyzed the classic studies. In Milgram's lab, people tended to continue when prodded in the name of the science ("The experiment requires that you continue") but typically refused a bare order ("You have no other choice, you must go on"). They argue that people follow authorities when they identify with them and believe they're right. Obedience, on this view, is less about blind habit and more about shared belief.

title: The Big Five
objective: After this level you can explain the five personality traits psychologists measure and what each one describes.
summary: Most psychologists describe personality with five traits, OCEAN. Each is a dial on which most people sit midway, usually measured by self-report, and the five appear across 50 cultures.

cards.headline: The dictionary holds about 4,500 words for what a person is like.
cards.body: In 1936 Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert combed an English dictionary for words that describe lasting personality traits, and found about 4,500 of them. Shy, careful, bossy, warm: the list goes on and on. Could a pile that big boil down to a few basics?

cards.headline: Five dials, not five boxes
cards.body: Today the most popular answer in personality psychology is the Five Factor Model, or Big Five. Its traits spell OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Everyone has all five. Each runs along a spectrum, and most of us sit somewhere midway rather than at either end. So you aren't simply an extravert or not; you sit somewhere on the extraversion dial.

title: What's Wrong With Personality Types
objective: After this level you can explain why type tests like the Myers-Briggs score poorly on reliability compared with trait measures.
summary: The Myers-Briggs sorts people into 16 types, but most people score near the middle of its scales, so types often flip on retest. Big Five scores stay closely matched.

cards.headline: Take the same personality test twice. You might come back a different type.
cards.body: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into one of 16 personality types. Yet in a 1993 review, psychologist David Pittenger reported that as many as 50 percent of people get a different type when retested only five weeks later. How could a personality change in five weeks?

cards.headline: Sixteen boxes from Jung
cards.body: The Myers-Briggs was developed by Isabel Briggs Myers and her mother, Katharine Briggs, after Katharine read Carl Jung's work on psychological types. It asks about four pairs of opposite preferences, such as extraversion versus introversion, and gives you one side of each pair. Combine the four and you land in one of 16 types, each labeled with four letters.

cards.headline: The crowded middle
cards.body: Boxes assume people split into two camps on each pair. But on the Myers-Briggs scales, most people score between the two extremes, and a cut-off point divides each scale. So two people with nearly identical scores can get opposite letters. If you sit near the cut-off, a small change in how you answer on a given day can flip a letter, and with it your whole type.

cards.headline: Why dials hold steadier
cards.body: A test's reliability is its consistency: it should give the same result each time it measures the same thing. In 1989, Robert McCrae and Paul Costa found no support for truly either-or Myers-Briggs preferences, although its four scales tracked four of the Big Five. Trait measures keep the score on the dial instead. Retest scores on the NEO PI-R, a widely used Big Five questionnaire, stay closely matched over weeks and even years.

title: Does Personality Change?
objective: After this level you can explain how stable personality is across a lifetime and how it tends to mature.
summary: Personality is partly heritable and keeps a steady rank order, yet on average people grow more conscientious and emotionally stable, especially between 20 and 40.

cards.headline: Will you still be the same person when you're old?
cards.body: Some say people never change; others say everyone reinvents themselves. Psychologists answered the slow way, by measuring the same traits again and again over years. The answer turns out to be both, depending on which kind of change you mean.

cards.headline: Some of it starts in the genes
cards.body: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart ran from 1979 to 1999. It found that identical twins have very similar personalities whether they were raised together or apart. That's the twin-study logic from Level 7 at work: when identical twins match even after growing up in different homes, genes likely play a part.

cards.headline: Everyone matures a little
cards.body: Yet traits still move. In 2006, Brent Roberts and colleagues pooled 92 samples of people measured over time. On average, people grew more conscientious, more emotionally stable and more socially assertive, especially between ages 20 and 40. Agreeableness changed only in old age. In short: across adulthood, the typical person gets more reliable and calmer.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. The whole group shifts with age, while each person tends to keep their place in line. Both are true.

cards.headline: You keep your place in line
cards.body: There's a second kind of stability: your rank compared with other people. A 2000 review by Brent Roberts and Wendy DelVecchio found that how consistently people keep their rank on traits grows from childhood through the college years and age 30, then levels off between 50 and 70. So a whole group can mature together while the most outgoing person in it stays among the most outgoing.

title: What IQ Tests Measure
objective: After this level you can explain what IQ tests measure, what scores predict, and why average scores rose over the 20th century.
summary: IQ tests score abilities like verbal comprehension and working memory against an average of 100. They predict grades only partly, and average scores rose about three points per decade.

cards.headline: The first intelligence test wasn't built to crown geniuses.
cards.body: In 1905, Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon in France published the first practical intelligence test. Its job was humble: to identify schoolchildren who needed extra help. So what do today's IQ tests actually measure, and what can a score tell you?

cards.headline: Inside an IQ test
cards.body: Modern tests such as the Wechsler scales give scores for areas like verbal comprehension, working memory and processing speed, then combine them. On most IQ tests the average is set at 100. To keep it there, tests are periodically recalibrated against new groups of test takers, like a ruler that gets checked against a fresh standard every so often.

cards.headline: What a score predicts
cards.body: IQ scores do predict school grades, but only partly. A 1996 American Psychological Association report led by Ulric Neisser found IQ explains only about a quarter of the differences in grades. Persistence, interest in school and willingness to study matter too. A score describes how someone did on a test, not the whole story of how they'll do in school.

cards.headline: Every generation scored higher
cards.body: Those recalibrations revealed a surprise: across the 20th century, average IQ scores rose about three points per decade. It's called the Flynn effect, after James Flynn. Genes can't be the main story: a 2018 study of Norwegian men found the rise, and a later dip, among brothers in the same families, pointing to the environment. Better nutrition, more schooling and a more complex world are leading suspects; the question remains unresolved.

title: Stress Lives in the Appraisal
objective: After this level you can explain how the way you judge a demand and your resources shapes how stressful it feels.
summary: In Lazarus and Folkman's view, stress follows appraisal: judging a threat or challenge, then your resources. A 1964 film study showed a new framing changes the body's stress response.

cards.headline: Same event, different stress. The difference is in your head.
cards.body: Two people can face the same bad news and react very differently. Psychologists Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman explained why: stress is a process in which people respond to events they appraise, or judge, as overwhelming or threatening. So what exactly are we judging?

cards.headline: Two quick judgments
cards.body: First comes a primary appraisal: how much harm or threat does this hold? The same event can be seen as a threat, a possible loss, or as a challenge, a chance to gain or grow. Then comes a secondary appraisal: what options do I have to cope, and how well will they work? A job interview can feel like a threat or a challenge depending on how you answer both.

cards.headline: When demands outrun resources
cards.body: Put the two together and you get the core rule: people feel stressed when they judge an event as harmful and believe its demands exceed their resources to handle it. Not all stress is bad, though. Eustress is good stress that motivates performance; distress is stress so excessive that performance declines. The same exam can push one student and flatten another.

mascot.line: This is Level 6's idea at work: the mind processes information, and how it reads an event shapes what happens next.

cards.headline: Change the story, change the body
cards.body: Lazarus tested the idea in the lab. In a 1964 study led by Joseph Speisman, people watched the same stressful film with different soundtracks. A soundtrack that stressed the threat raised their skin conductance, a bodily sign of stress. Soundtracks that offered calmer interpretations lowered it. Same film, different appraisal, different body.

title: Coping That Helps
objective: After this level you can compare problem-focused and emotion-focused coping and judge which fits a given situation.
summary: Problem-focused coping changes the problem; emotion-focused coping eases the feelings. Coping may work best when it fits how controllable a stressor is, with partial support in tests.

cards.headline: You can fix the leak, or keep calm while it rains. Both count as coping.
cards.body: Coping means the mental and behavioral efforts people use to deal with stress. Psychologists sort those efforts into two broad families. The interesting question is which one to reach for, and when.

items.label: Problem-focused
points: Tries to manage or change the problem itself
Example: getting tutoring for a hard class

items.label: Emotion-focused
points: Tries to reduce the negative emotions

cards.headline: Controllable or not?
cards.body: Many stressors draw both kinds of coping. But people lean on problem-focused coping when they see a stressor as controllable, and on emotion-focused coping when they feel powerless to change it. You can study for a retake. You can't make exam results arrive sooner, but you can calm your nerves while you wait.

cards.headline: Does matching really help?
cards.body: The goodness-of-fit hypothesis, from Lazarus and Folkman, says coping works best when it matches how controllable a stressor is. In a 2004 study, 190 students reported their most stressful event every day for 28 days. Problem-focused coping went with better mood more strongly when the stressor was controllable. Other tests found only partial support, so treat fit as a sensible guide rather than a law.

title: Bouncing Back
objective: After this level you can explain what research on loss and hardship shows about how common resilience is.
summary: Resilience, staying fairly stable through loss or trauma, differs from recovery and is common: about 46 percent after a spouse's death in one study, and 65 percent after September 11.

cards.headline: Experts once saw calm after a loss as a warning sign.
cards.body: In a 1993 survey, 65 percent of self-identified bereavement experts said that absent grief usually stems from denial and is harmful in the long run. If someone seemed to cope well after a death, the thinking went, the grief was just hidden. Then researchers started following people through loss and checking.

mascot.line: Keep the difference: recovery dips and climbs back, while resilience bends without a long slump.

cards.headline: Resilience isn't recovery
cards.body: In 2004, psychologist George Bonanno drew a line between two paths. In recovery, a person's functioning drops for months or longer, then returns. In resilience, a person keeps relatively stable, healthy functioning through the loss or a potentially traumatic event. Resilient people still have rough patches, such as several weeks of restless sleep, but they don't fall into a long slump.

cards.headline: Checking before the loss
cards.body: Most grief studies begin after a death, so nobody knows what people were like before. One prospective study had data from about three years before a spouse died. About 46 percent of participants had low depression before the loss and 18 months after, and they weren't cold or distant. No clear sign of delayed grief appeared, and most still felt pangs of yearning. Resilience isn't feeling nothing.

cards.fact: After the September 11 attacks, about 65 percent of New York-area residents in one large study were resilient.
cards.context: In 2006, George Bonanno and colleagues studied 2,752 people in the six months after the attacks. Resilience was less common among the most exposed, yet it never fell below about a third in any group. Resilience turned out to be the rule, not the rare exception.

title: What Happiness Research Finds
objective: After this level you can explain hedonic adaptation and why relationships predict wellbeing better than windfalls.
summary: People adapt to good and bad changes, so lottery wins fade, though some events leave lasting marks. The happiest people stand out for strong relationships, not more good events.

cards.headline: Winning the lottery doesn't make people as happy as you'd think.
cards.body: In 1978, Philip Brickman and colleagues interviewed 22 major lottery winners and 22 comparison people. The winners weren't happier than the comparison group, and they took less pleasure from everyday events. Where did the joy go?

cards.headline: The fading glow
cards.body: Psychologists call it hedonic adaptation: over time, the joys and sorrows that follow good and bad events fade. Brickman's team proposed two forces behind it. Contrast: after the thrill of winning, ordinary pleasures feel smaller. Habituation: new pleasures slowly lose their value. The new car is thrilling in its first weeks, and later it's just your car.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the list of events. Remember the shape: adaptation is common, but not guaranteed.

cards.headline: But not everything fades
cards.body: Adaptation isn't guaranteed. A 2007 review by Richard Lucas found that divorce, a spouse's death, unemployment and disability are linked to lasting changes in wellbeing, and that people differ in how fully they adapt. The glow fades after a windfall; some hard events leave a longer mark.

cards.headline: What the happiest share
cards.body: So what sets very happy people apart? In 2002, Ed Diener and Martin Seligman compared the happiest 10 percent of 222 students with average and very unhappy students, combining the students' own reports, gathered over months and daily for 51 days, with reports from their peers. The happiest had stronger social relationships and were more extraverted. They didn't have more good events. Good relationships were necessary, but not enough on their own.
